content: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory condition that affects approximately 300 million individuals globally. Yoga, as a holistic therapeutic approach, has gained popularity worldwide for its potential to alleviate both the physical and psychological burdens associated with asthma. Numerous clinical trials have been conducted to evaluate the effects of yoga on asthma, but the results have been inconsistent. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of yoga on individuals with asthma. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted using the Cochrane Airways Group Register of Trials, which includes data from various bibliographic databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, AMED, and PsycINFO, as well as handsearching respiratory journals and meeting abstracts. Additional searches were performed on PEDro, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO ICTRP search portal. The search covered all databases from their inception up to July 22, 2015, without any language restrictions. Reference lists of eligible studies and relevant reviews were also examined, and investigators and experts in the field were contacted to identify additional published or unpublished studies. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared yoga interventions with usual care, no intervention, or sham interventions in individuals with asthma. Eligible studies reported at least one of the following outcomes: quality of life, asthma symptom scores, asthma control, lung function measures, asthma medication usage, or adverse events. Data were extracted on study characteristics, participant demographics, intervention details, and outcomes of interest. For continuous outcomes measured on the same scale, mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. For outcomes measured on different scales, standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% CI were used. For dichotomous outcomes, risk ratios (RR) with 95% CI were calculated. Meta-analyses were performed using Review Manager 5.3, employing a fixed-effect model unless substantial heterogeneity was present, in which case a random-effects model was used. Outcomes that could not be pooled quantitatively were analyzed descriptively. Fifteen RCTs involving a total of 1,048 participants were included in the review. Most studies were conducted in India, with others in Europe and the United States. Participants were predominantly adults of both sexes with mild to moderate asthma, with disease duration ranging from six months to over 23 years. Five studies focused solely on yoga breathing techniques, while the remaining studies included a combination of breathing exercises, postures, and meditation. Intervention durations ranged from two weeks to 54 months, with most lasting no more than six months. The risk of bias was low across all domains in one study, but unclear or high in at least one domain in the remaining studies. The findings suggested that yoga may lead to improvements in quality of life, as measured by the Asthma Quality of Life Questionnaire (AQLQ). The mean difference in AQLQ scores was 0.57 units on a 7-point scale (95% CI 0.37 to 0.77) across five studies involving 375 participants. This exceeded the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of 0.5. Yoga also appeared to improve asthma symptoms (SMD 0.37, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.65; three studies; 243 participants) and reduce medication usage (RR 5.35, 95% CI 1.29 to 22.11; two studies). However, the clinical significance of the symptom improvements was uncertain due to the lack of an established MCID for the severity scores used in the included studies. Yoga did not demonstrate statistically significant effects on lung function, as measured by changes in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) from baseline (MD 0.04 liters, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.19; seven studies; 340 participants; I² = 68%). Two studies reported improved asthma control, but the data could not be pooled due to substantial heterogeneity (I² = 98%). No serious adverse events related to yoga were reported, but the data on adverse events were limited. In conclusion, moderate-quality evidence suggests that yoga may result in small improvements in quality of life and asthma symptoms. However, there is considerable uncertainty regarding its effects on lung function, medication usage, and potential adverse events. Further high-quality RCTs with larger sample sizes and rigorous methodological standards are needed to confirm the effects of yoga on asthma.
